finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id removes any report without an effective authorization check, because authorize() is called without await.
finding.source: Any request to DELETE /reports/:id. req.user comes from req.session.user (server.js:5); report id from req.params.id (server.js:19). Caller may be unauthenticated.

trace.note: DELETE handler starts; req.params.id used as report id
authorize(req.user,'delete',report) called without await; returns pending promise
authorize awaits db.grants; throws 403 only after that resolves
remove issued immediately, regardless of grant outcome

finding.guards_checked: authorize() grant check (server.js:9-16) exists but its result never gates the delete; no route-level auth middleware in this file; no null check on req.user. If req.user is undefined, authorize throws a TypeError that is also an unhandled rejection, and the delete still runs. On Node 15+ the unhandled rejection can crash the process (DoS).

verdict.guard_found: None effective. server.js:9-16 authorize() does throw on a failed grant, but server.js:20 calls it without await, so its rejection is never observed before server.js:21 runs. No route-level auth middleware is present; server.js:4-7 only copies req.session.user onto req.user and does not reject unauthenticated requests. The PUT handler at server.js:27 uses await and is not affected.
verdict.reason: At server.js:20 authorize() returns a pending promise at its first await (server.js:10), so execution continues to server.js:21 and db.reports.remove runs whether or not the grant check at server.js:11-14 fails. The trace is accurate. Reachability depends on whether session middleware, which is not in this file, lets an unauthenticated caller reach the route, and if req.session is missing, server.js:5 throws and the handler never runs.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the whole request body to db.reports.update, enabling mass assignment of any column by a user who holds 'write'.
finding.source: req.body parsed by express.json() (server.js:3) from any PUT /reports/:id request

trace.note: express.json() parses body into req.body with no field allowlist
authorize(...,'write',report) is awaited and gates this route
entire req.body passed to update() as the fields to write

finding.guards_checked: Write authorization correctly awaited at server.js:27, so unauthenticated writes are blocked. No field allowlist or schema validation in this file. DB schema not visible, so whether owner/grant/id columns are writable is unconfirmed; severity depends on that.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)`. authorize (server.js:9-16) throws a 403 when the grant for "write" is missing, and the throw propagates because the call is awaited, so the update at server.js:28 is not reached without the grant. server.js:20 (the DELETE route) is a bare un-awaited call, but that is a separate route and does not affect PUT. No field allowlist or schema validation exists in server.js.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: req.body is parsed at server.js:3 and passed unfiltered to update at server.js:28 after the awaited write check at server.js:27 (which throws, so it is effective). The attacker must already hold a "write" grant on that specific report, so the only added power is writing non-content columns (owner, id, grant-related fields), and db is not defined in the provided files (only server.js is present), so whether any such column exists and is writable cannot be determined.

finding.claim: PUT and DELETE rely on session auth with no visible CSRF protection, so a cross-site page could trigger them with the victim's session cookie.
finding.source: Cross-site form or fetch from an attacker-controlled page, sent with the victim's session cookie
finding.sink: State changes at server.js:18 (DELETE) and server.js:25 (PUT)

trace.note: req.user taken from session with no CSRF token or Origin/Referer check

finding.guards_checked: No CSRF middleware in this file. Cookie SameSite attributes live in session middleware not visible here, so this is unconfirmed. Likely mitigated if the cookie is SameSite=Lax or Strict.

verdict.guard_found: Browser-enforced limits on cross-site PUT/DELETE, which the server does not disable. HTML forms can only send GET or POST, so the attacker cannot send a cross-site form PUT or DELETE. A cross-origin fetch with PUT or DELETE is non-simple and needs a CORS preflight. server.js has no OPTIONS handler and no cors middleware (lines 1-32), so the preflight fails and the state-changing request is never sent. No CSRF token or Origin/Referer check exists in this file; the SameSite setting lives in session middleware that is not in this file, so it is unknown.
verdict.reason: The exploit path needs a cross-site PUT or DELETE carrying the session cookie, but HTML forms cannot send those methods and the non-simple fetch fails preflight because server.js:18-30 defines no OPTIONS handling or CORS headers, so the candidate's mechanism is not reachable from a browser; trace_ok is false only because the candidate cites server.js:4 for the req.user assignment, which is on line 5. Separately, server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so the DELETE at line 21 runs even when the check throws. That is a real authorization bug, but it is not CSRF and it is out of scope for this candidate.
